text: Sri Lanka will reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 14.5% against the business-as-usual scenario by 2030, of which 4% is unconditional and 10.5% is conditional on international support.
The Government commits to achieving net zero emissions by 2050 across all sectors of the economy.
Renewable energy will account for 70% of national electricity generation by 2030, up from 35% in 2020.
Unabated coal-fired power stations will be retired from the generation fleet no later than 2035.
An economy-wide emissions trading scheme will be introduced with an absolute cap declining by 4% annually.
A carbon price floor of USD 45 per tonne will apply to the power and industrial sectors from 2027.
Fossil fuel subsidies will be phased out by 2027 and the fiscal savings redirected to social protection.
The carbon intensity of the electricity grid will fall to 100 grams of CO2 per kilowatt hour by 2035.
Coastal protection works will be constructed along 120 km of shoreline to defend communities against sea level rise and storm surge.
A national multi-hazard early warning system will be established to give at-risk communities advance notice of floods, cyclones and drought.
Vulnerability and risk assessments will be completed for all coastal districts before the end of the plan period.
Mangrove and wetland ecosystems will be restored to buffer inland areas from tidal surge and saline intrusion.
Urban drainage infrastructure will be upgraded to withstand a one-in-fifty-year rainfall event.
Heat action plans will be prepared for the twelve largest cities to reduce mortality during extreme heat episodes.
The total investment required to deliver the mitigation component is estimated at USD 12.6 billion over the period to 2030.
The Government will issue sovereign green bonds and establish a blended finance facility to crowd in private capital.
Access to the Green Climate Fund and bilateral concessional loans will be pursued to close the adaptation financing gap.
An annual budget allocation of LKR 45 billion is committed to the adaptation programme for the first three years.
Public financial institutions will be required to disclose the climate risk exposure of their lending portfolios.
The Climate Change Act 2023 establishes legally binding five-year carbon budgets and creates a duty on ministers to meet them.
A National Climate Change Council chaired by the Prime Minister will coordinate implementation across ministries.
The Ministry of Environment is designated as the national focal point and is mandated to enforce compliance with the regulations made under this Act.
Climate objectives will be mainstreamed into the national development plan and all sectoral investment appraisals.
Failure to comply with the emissions reporting obligation is an offence punishable by a fine not exceeding one million rupees.
A measurement, reporting and verification system will be established to track emissions across all covered sectors.
The national greenhouse gas inventory will be updated annually and progress will be reported biennially in line with the enhanced transparency framework.
Indicators, baselines and milestones will be defined for each measure so that delivery can be independently audited.
An independent expert committee will review progress every two years and lay its report before Parliament.
Emissions from road transport will be reduced through electrification of the public bus fleet and expansion of urban rail.
Methane emissions from paddy cultivation and livestock will be addressed through improved water management and feed practices.
Landfill gas capture will be installed at all municipal waste sites serving populations above 100,000.
Forest cover will be increased to 32% of land area through reforestation and protection of existing carbon sinks.
Minimum energy performance standards will apply to all new commercial and residential buildings from 2026.
Clinker substitution and alternative fuels will reduce process emissions from domestic cement manufacture.
A just transition programme will provide retraining and income support to workers displaced from coal-dependent industries.
The rights, knowledge and free prior informed consent of indigenous and local communities will be respected in all land-based measures.
Gender-responsive budgeting will be applied so that women and youth benefit equitably from climate investments.
Targeted energy bill support will protect low-income households from the distributional impact of the carbon levy.
Green hydrogen production and grid-scale battery storage will be supported through targeted research and development funding.
Carbon capture, utilisation and storage will be demonstrated at two industrial sites by 2032.
Technology transfer arrangements and technical capacity building will be sought from development partners.
A national innovation fund will co-finance demonstration projects for low-carbon industrial processes.
This contribution is submitted in accordance with Article 4 of the Paris Agreement and the decisions of the Conference of the Parties.
The country will engage in Article 6.2 cooperative approaches while ensuring that internationally transferred mitigation outcomes are not double counted.
Bilateral partnerships with regional neighbours will be pursued on shared river basin management and disaster response.
The outcome of the first global stocktake has informed the level of ambition set out in this contribution.
Energy intensity of GDP will be reduced by 25% by 2035 relative to 2020 through industrial efficiency standards.
Public health systems will be strengthened to respond to heat stress and the expanding range of vector-borne disease.
Climate-resilient crop varieties will be distributed to smallholder farmers in drought-prone districts.
USD 800 million of concessional finance will be directed to coastal defence works protecting vulnerable fishing communities.

The country will cut greenhouse gas emissions by 45% below 2005 levels by 2030 as its nationally determined contribution.
Carbon neutrality across the whole economy is targeted no later than 2060.
Installed solar and wind capacity will reach 5,000 MW by 2032, tripling the current renewable fleet.
Routine flaring of associated gas at upstream facilities will end by 2030.
A low-emission development strategy to 2060 will be prepared and submitted to the secretariat.
Hydrofluorocarbon consumption will be reduced in line with obligations under the Kigali Amendment.
Absolute emissions from the power sector will peak before 2028 and decline thereafter.
Sea walls and revetments will be reinforced at seventeen locations identified as at highest risk of inundation.
Water storage capacity will be expanded to secure supply through longer and more frequent dry seasons.
A national adaptation plan will be prepared, setting out priority actions to reduce vulnerability to climate impacts.
Disaster risk reduction measures will be integrated into local government planning in all flood-prone municipalities.
Climate risk screening will become a mandatory step in the appraisal of all major infrastructure projects.
Insurance and social safety net instruments will be developed to help farmers absorb climate-related crop losses.
Delivery of the plan requires an estimated USD 3.4 billion, of which USD 2.1 billion is expected from international sources.
A dedicated National Climate Fund will be capitalised from levy receipts and managed under Treasury oversight.
Commercial banks will be incentivised to expand green lending through a preferential reserve requirement.
Total adaptation costs are projected at 1.2% of GDP annually through to 2040.
Parliament shall enact primary legislation giving statutory force to the emissions targets set out in this strategy.
An inter-ministerial steering committee will be constituted within six months of publication.
Provincial authorities are empowered to make by-laws consistent with the national framework.
The regulator will be granted powers of inspection, enforcement and the imposition of administrative penalties.
Facilities emitting more than 25,000 tonnes of CO2 equivalent per year must report annually to the national registry.
A digital monitoring platform will consolidate activity data from all reporting entities into a single register.
Third-party verification of reported emissions will be mandatory from the second compliance period.
Progress against each indicator will be published on a public dashboard updated every quarter.
Rail freight's share of inland tonne-kilometres will be raised from 8% to 20% by 2035.
Nitrogen fertiliser use efficiency will be improved through precision application in the arable sector.
Separate collection of organic waste will be mandatory in all urban local authorities by 2029.
Domestic aviation and coastal shipping will be brought within the scope of the reporting obligation.
Degraded peatlands will be rewetted to halt ongoing carbon losses from drained organic soils.
Communities dependent on peat extraction will receive transition support and alternative livelihood funding.
Consultation with affected workers and trade unions will precede the closure of any state-owned facility.
Persons with disabilities and the elderly will be prioritised in heatwave and flood response planning.
Energy poverty will be monitored as an explicit indicator of a fair transition.
Pilot deployment of direct air capture will be assessed for technical and economic feasibility.
Smart grid and demand-response technologies will be rolled out to accommodate variable renewable generation.
A national centre of excellence for climate research will be established at the state university.
Support will be sought under the Technology Mechanism for capacity building in emissions modelling.
The country reaffirms its commitment to the temperature goal of Article 2 of the Paris Agreement.
Regional cooperation on transboundary haze and forest fire management will be strengthened.
The conditional element of this target is contingent on the provision of international climate finance and technology transfer.
Biennial transparency reports will be submitted in accordance with the modalities, procedures and guidelines agreed at COP24.
District heating networks will be converted from coal to waste heat and heat pumps by 2033.
Public procurement rules will require embodied carbon assessment for all construction contracts above the threshold.
